extracted.intended_audience: district court judges, patent litigators, damages experts, and trial practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Model and recommended jury instructions and substantive criteria for calculating reasonable royalty patent damages (including SEP/[F]RAND issues), focusing on factors juries should consider and how to perform/apportion damages calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smallest saleable unit anchoring / apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: The smallest saleable patent-practicing unit requirement is intended to establish the 'anchor' closest to the patented technology and is a step toward meeting the requirement of apportionment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the smallest saleable unit as the anchor to avoid overvaluing the patent by including value of other components; where the smallest saleable unit is a multi-component product, the patentee must estimate what portion of that product's value is attributable to the patented technology. Courts should resist using the end-product price as the anchor absent a clear method for apportioning non-patented value. Juries may consider evidence that a component's market price is misleadingly low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparable agreements (Factor Three)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury should consider prior agreements by the patent holder to license the patent(s)-in-suit or other agreements if they were negotiated in circumstances, and concerned subjects, sufficiently comparable to those that would be involved in the parties' negotiation regarding the patent(s)-in-suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The offering party bears the burden to show technological and economic comparability by comparing technology, scope, context, and value of the prior license to the pre-investment hypothetical license; licenses need not be identical but must be more than loosely or vaguely comparable. Examples/citations show courts rejecting licenses that bear no discernible link to the claimed technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic comparability and package discounts
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing economic comparability, the jury should be cautioned that the royalty stated in an agreement will not necessarily reflect the true market price of the licensed patent if the agreement included other consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a license was part of a broader package (e.g., cross-licenses, other services), the stated royalty might exaggerate the true consideration for the patent itself; the jury should account for that by allocating the package consideration appropriately or discounting where warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex post licenses and lock-in distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Licenses negotiated after the licensee had invested in the technology (ex post) may be inflated by lock-in costs and therefore fail to capture the true market value at the ex ante hypothetical negotiation date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should instruct juries to treat ex post licenses with caution (and generally exclude litigation settlement agreements). If such agreements are admitted, juries should be told they are disfavored because they tend to overstate patent value due to lock-in and litigation-related considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement agreements generally disfavored as comparables
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigation settlement agreements are shaped by ex post considerations and are therefore unsuitable to prove the amount of a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement payments made in coercive litigation contexts should generally be excluded; if admitted, instruct jurors that such agreements may be tainted and likely overstate value. Cite historical and case-law authority supporting exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude discounts caused by uncertainty as to validity or infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patent holder proves that a stated royalty included a discount because of uncertainty as to whether the patent(s)-in-suit were valid and infringed, the court should instruct the jury to exclude that discount in the reasonable royalty determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust comparable-license evidence to remove reductions that reflect risk/uncertainty rather than market value of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial considerations showing willingness or reluctance to license (Factor Four)
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensor's relative willingness to license can be relevant to assessing a reasonable royalty; licensing eagerness or reluctance affects the bargaining outcome and thus the royalty the parties would have agreed to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If licensor would have willingly licensed ex ante, parties would bargain to divide the incremental value up to the incremental value over the infringer's best alternative. If licensor would have been unwilling (e.g., policy not to license or only under special conditions), the jury may find a higher royalty, up to the incremental value. Avoid treating strategic delay to extract a better deal as true unwillingness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish strategic delay from true unwillingness to license
rubrics_metrics.description: A party should not be treated as an 'unwilling' licensor if it was willing to license ex ante but delayed for strategic reasons to obtain a better deal later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of intent to license eventually but to wait for lock-in is not a basis to avoid deeming the licensor a willing licensor; courts should not allow licensors to benefit from such strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider inventor-promoter relationships and FRAND constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain commercial relationships (e.g., inventor-promoter) or commitments (SSO FRAND assurances) may affect the parties' relative willingness to license and thus the reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent is subject to a FRAND commitment, the patentee must be considered a willing, non-discriminatory licensor. Jury instructions should include relevant assurance or SSO policy language and require the jury to take the FRAND commitment into account when determining reasonable royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-standard negotiation date for SEPs (date of hypothetical negotiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For patents essential to a standard and subject to a FRAND commitment, the hypothetical negotiation date must be just before the patented technology was incorporated into the standard (the 'pre-standard negotiation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruct juries to use the date the patent became essential to the standard rather than the implementer's date of first use; base royalties on the contribution of the patented technology to the standard and the contribution of that capability to the implementer's products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude value contributed by other patents/brand/marketing in FRAND cases (Factor Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: When computing a royalty for SEPs/FRAND-encumbered patents, the royalty should reflect only the contribution of the patented technology itself and not value contributed by other patents, technologies, product marketing, or brand recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apportion the value properly to avoid awarding the patent holder value attributable to the standard as a whole, other patents in the standard, or the implementer's commercial advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of royalties — lump sum vs running royalties
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury should be instructed on the difference between lump sum payments (single payment covering all sales) and running royalties (payment per unit or percentage of sales), and choose which structure fits the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain advantages of lump sum (certainty, avoid monitoring) versus running royalty (ongoing per-sale payments). For running royalties, identify appropriate royalty base (e.g., smallest saleable unit or entire market value) and royalty rate. Jury must select the structure based on case evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: No enhancement for post-verdict infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: No enhancement of the reasonable royalty should be awarded for post-verdict infringement because the hypothetical negotiation already assumes validity and infringement and generally would have covered post-verdict periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not increase royalties to punish or to account for post-verdict changes; only in rare cases where the ex ante license would clearly have been for a more limited period should the jury determine subsequent-year royalties using the same ex ante criteria at a later negotiation date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide juries simple quantitative damages methods and options
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond qualitative factors, juries should be given simple quantitative methods for calculating a specific damages number, including formulas and options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may provide a calculation form and the jury's task can be limited to determining inputs; courts can present competing methodologies as options. The verdict form should require the jury to 'show its work' by identifying the method used and inputs, facilitating appellate review and avoiding 'black box' awards. The court must exclude methodologies that do not answer the correct legal question (ex ante incremental-value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court gatekeeping over acceptable damages methodologies
rubrics_metrics.description: The court must keep from the jury any methodologies not reasonably calculated to answer the correct legal question — the royalty the parties would have agreed to in the hypothetical ex ante negotiation, exclusive of ex post considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude methodologies that rely on lock-in, litigation risk, or other ex post factors, and ensure presented methods are tethered to the best alternative available at the ex ante date and proper apportionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customize instructions to the facts; define non-infringing alternatives concretely
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic recitation of factors is often too abstract; instructions should be tailored to the facts, e.g., explicitly telling the jury what a ‘non-infringing alternative’ is in the case and how the defendant alleges a particular alternative affects the royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific, case-tied wording: identify the alleged non-infringing alternative, state whether it was available at the relevant negotiation date, and instruct that any royalty must be based on the incremental value of the claimed invention over that commercially acceptable alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus jury on ex ante incremental value over best alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury instructions should consistently focus the jury on determining the ex ante incremental value of the patented technology over the alleged infringer's best alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating numerous ex post considerations as primary; prioritize apportionment to the incremental contribution and ensure jurors do not award damages based on lock-in costs, litigation risk, or the value of the standard itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruct jurors on apportionment and value of non-patented factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Juries should be expressly instructed to consider the value added by other patented technologies embodied in the accused product, as well as non-patented factors such as manufacturing process, product marketing, or brand recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit apportionment instructions help prevent jurors from overvaluing the patent-in-suit relative to other essential components; explain how these other contributions affect the reasonable royalty calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider probative value of prior licenses and licensor's pre-investment willingness
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury should focus on the probative value of prior license agreements and commercial evidence that indicate the licensor's relative willingness ex ante to enter an agreement with the alleged infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While prior licenses are often highly relevant to market value, instruct juries to account for ex post distortions (e.g., lock-in) and to weigh whether those licenses reflect real-world fair-market value at the ex ante date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use verdict form to capture methodology and inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: The verdict form should require the jury to identify the specific damages method used and the inputs relied upon, effectively showing its work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including the calculation methodologies as explicit options on the verdict form facilitates appellate review, reduces black-box awards, and clarifies the basis for the damages determination.
